opus-5.5.text:
I think the core goal is quite practical: make long-context inference cheaper without giving up quality. With standard softmax attention, the KV cache grows linearly with sequence length, and the compute for each new token grows with it. That gets very expensive as we push toward long contexts, agentic workloads, and long reasoning traces, where the model generates huge numbers of tokens. Decoding then becomes memory-bound, and the KV cache is basically the bottleneck.

So the idea is to replace most of the full-attention layers with a linear-attention-style layer that keeps a fixed-size recurrent state instead of an ever-growing cache. Kimi's variant builds on the delta rule line of work, things like DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet. The delta rule makes the state behave less like a bucket you keep dumping information into and more like an associative memory you actually *update*: you can overwrite or correct what's stored for a given key. Adding gating, and in Kimi's case finer-grained gating, lets the model decide more precisely what to forget and how fast, which matters a lot because a fixed-size state has limited capacity.

But they didn't go fully linear, and I think that's the honest part of the design. Pure linear attention still struggles with precise retrieval, like copying or finding a needle in a long context. So they use a hybrid: mostly linear layers, with a few full-attention layers interleaved to handle exact lookup. You get most of the efficiency, a much smaller KV cache and higher decoding throughput, while the occasional global attention layers cover the retrieval weaknesses.

So in one sentence: the goal isn't to eliminate attention, it's to rebalance the architecture so that most of the "memory work" happens in an efficient, expressive recurrent state, and you only pay the full quadratic price where you really need it. And it's significant that a lab is validating this at real scale, because for a long time the question about these architectures was "does it hold up when you actually train a big model on it?"

r001.rationale: It says long-context inference should be cheaper “without giving up quality,” which communicates avoiding performance degradation relative to full attention.

r002.rationale: It mentions higher decoding throughput, but does not say inference is many times faster than full attention.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the core goal is actually pretty simple to state, even if the engineering is hard: make attention cheaper at long context without giving up the things that make full attention good.

If you look at what Kimi did, the key move is a hybrid. Most layers use a linear attention variant, and only a small fraction keep full softmax attention. The reason you want that mix is that linear attention has a fixed-size state, so it doesn't blow up in memory as the sequence grows and decoding stays fast. But a fixed-size state is also a lossy summary. It compresses, and some things genuinely need precise retrieval, like finding an exact token or copying a long span. Those few full attention layers act as the lookup mechanism. So you keep the expensive, precise part sparse and let the cheap, compressive part handle most of the work.

What I find interesting is that the design question isn't really "linear versus softmax." It's "how much of each, and where." Their ablations suggest something like a three-to-one ratio works, and that you can replace most layers without losing quality on standard benchmarks. That's an empirical claim about where the real information-routing bottlenecks live in a transformer.

The other piece people sometimes miss is that this is also about training efficiency, not just inference. If you want to scale context to a million tokens during pretraining or RL, the attention cost dominates. Reducing that lets you train on longer sequences for the same budget, and in the agentic setting, where models generate very long trajectories, decode speed matters a lot. So I'd summarize the goal as: shift the cost structure of the model so long-context becomes economically viable at scale, while keeping the retrieval capabilities you can't recover once you throw them away.

r001.rationale: The response says the design aims to avoid giving up full attention’s strengths and notes that most layers can be replaced without losing benchmark quality.

r002.rationale: It describes decoding as fast and attention as cheaper, but does not clearly say inference is many times faster than with full attention.

astra-6.text:
My understanding is that the core goal is to make attention more efficient while preserving the model’s ability to use context. As the context gets longer, reading and attending to all of it becomes increasingly expensive. The question is whether we can spend that computation on the information that actually matters for the current prediction.

So I’d frame it as improving the trade-off between capability and cost: reducing the burden of long-context processing without losing important dependencies. The architecture change is a means to that end. The real test is whether the model can still retrieve, connect, and reason over relevant information reliably.

r001.rationale: The response says it aims to preserve context use and important dependencies, but does not identify performance preservation relative to full attention.

r002.rationale: It describes attention as becoming more efficient and reducing long-context processing costs, but does not say inference should be many times faster than full attention.
